cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Editing is the process of selecting, arranging and combining shots to construct narrative, meaning and emotional impact.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Continuity editing creates a seamless, invisible flow that maintains spatial and temporal coherence for the viewer.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: The 180-degree rule ensures the camera stays on one side of an imaginary line between characters to preserve screen direction and spatial consistency.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Shot-reverse-shot alternates between two characters in conversation, creating the impression of a natural conversational exchange.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Match on action cuts during a continuous movement so the action flows seamlessly across the cut, making the edit invisible.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Eyeline match cuts from a character looking off-screen to what they are looking at, establishing spatial relationships and directing audience attention.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Montage editing juxtaposes images to create new meaning through association, contrast or thematic connection rather than narrative continuity.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Soviet montage theory, developed by Eisenstein and Kuleshov, argues that meaning is created through the collision or juxtaposition of images rather than within individual shots.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Transitions include straight cuts, dissolves, fades and wipes, each carrying different connotations about time, space and narrative progression.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: A dissolve overlaps the end of one shot with the beginning of the next, often used to suggest a passage of time or thematic connection between scenes.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Pace refers to the rhythm of editing determined by shot duration: fast cutting creates tension and excitement while slow cutting creates calm or contemplation.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Editing
cards.back: Parallel editing or cross-cutting alternates between two or more simultaneous actions in different locations, building suspense and highlighting thematic connections.
